title: Mint Hibiscus Cooler (Bissap)
author: Pierre Thiam with Jennifer Sit (Lake Isle Press), article by Dara O’Brien
desc: Dried red hibiscus and mint brought to a boil in 2 cups of water, honey stirred in off the heat, the remaining quart added, infused 10 to 15 minutes, strained and chilled over ice.
longDesc: Thiam’s bissap, from ‘Senegal: Modern Senegalese Recipes From the Source to the Bowl’ (Lake Isle Press, 2015), is the clearest quantified hibiscus water in the research. In a saucepan 2 cups of the water, the hibiscus flowers and the mint are brought to a boil; the heat is turned off, the honey stirred in and the mixture left to cool; the remaining quart of water is added and the pitcher set aside to infuse 10 to 15 minutes; strained into a pitcher and refrigerated; served cold over ice, garnished with extra mint. The page’s own cultural line: hibiscus is native to West Africa and hibiscus water is one of Senegal’s most popular beverages; it is called ‘Agua de Jamaica’ in Mexico.
ingredients: 1/4 cup fresh mint leaves, plus extra sprigs for garnish
steps: In a saucepan, bring 2 cups of the water, the hibiscus flowers and the mint to a boil.
Turn off the heat, stir in the honey, and let cool.
Add the remaining 1 quart of water.
Set aside to infuse for 10 to 15 minutes.
Strain into a pitcher and refrigerate.
Serve cold over ice, garnished with extra mint.
chefTips: The only timing is the 10 to 15 minute infusion; no colour or taste cue is printed.
The method says ‘stir in the honey’ though the ingredient list offers ‘honey or sugar’ — the page does not say how to dissolve sugar instead.
‘1 quart plus 2 cups’ is the page’s own phrasing and has not been summed.
commonMistakes: Boiling all the water with the flowers; the method boils only 2 cups.
Leaving the flowers in the pitcher past the infusion.
Using the second recipe’s ratio (SEN106) with this one’s quantities — they differ about ten-fold.
storage: Refrigerated; no storage time is printed.
healthBenefits: Hibiscus is tart and rich in anthocyanins; honey or sugar is the sweetener.
culturalNote: ‘Also known as roselle, hibiscus is native to West Africa, and hibiscus water is one of Senegal’s most popular beverages.’ Compare the white-calyx bissap used in sauces and broths (see SEN098 note).
sources: Article title as printed: ‘Bissap (Hibiscus Water)’; recipe title as printed: ‘Mint Hibiscus Cooler (Hibiscus Water/Bissap)’. Article byline exactly as printed: ‘By Dara O’Brien,’ Creative Director, Lake Isle Press. Cookbook attribution as printed: ‘Senegal, Modern Senegalese Recipes From the Source to the Bowl’ by Pierre Thiam with Jennifer Sit, Lake Isle Press, 2015. Date: not shown on the page (the cookbook year is printed). Yield ‘Serves 6’. TWO-PASS, character-identical ingredients and method.
Reported as printed: fraction glyphs (¼, ½), ‘1 quart plus 2 cups’ not summed; ‘stir in the honey’ against ‘honey or sugar’. Cue: none, time only (10 to 15 minutes).

DISAGREEMENT with SEN106 (and with a rejected Nkosi Agro page: 35 g flowers to 2 litres for 8, off the heat, with ginger), not averaged: Thiam uses 1/4 pound hibiscus to 1 quart + 2 cups water for 6 and boils the flowers.
Prep 5, cook 5 and rest 25 are scheduling estimates (the 10 to 15 minute infusion plus unspecified cooling); not source data.
